newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FNB shares see-saw on renewed sale talk.
newsitem.headline: FNB shares see-saw on renewed sale talk.

text.p: Shares in First National Bank, one of South Africa's four biggest banks, have yo-yoed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange in the past two weeks on fresh rumours that a hefty stake in the firm is to be sold off.

FNB stocks reached a nine-month high of 30.80 rand on Tuesday, after a steady climb last week, but have lost over four percent of their value in the past two days to settle at 29.50 rand on Thursday as speculation began to wane.
An FNB spokeswoman said on Thursday there was no substance in the latest rumours.

Talk that Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd is set to sell off its 20.4 percent stake in FNB is nothing new and has been circulating in financial markets for months. The list of possible suitors continues to grow.

"The three suitors being mentioned are (South Africa's) Nedcor Ltd, although I think that is unlikely, Barclays of the UK and Hong Kong Shanghai Bank," said Dave Southey, a banking analyst at Edey Rogers.
Another name which has cropped up as a prospective buyer is South African financial group Investec Ltd, which lacks a retail base and is known for its acquisitiveness.

Barclays Plc which formerly owned FNB before withdrawing from South Africa in 1987, has long been viewed as a key candidate. The British bank two years ago again set up shop in South Africa, establishing a wholly-owned subsidiary focusing on commercial and investment business.
But London banking sources on Thursday played down a Barclays link-up saying the group had no immediate intention to have a retail presence in South Africa.
Barclays declined to comment. "This is market rumour and speculation and we don't comment on that," a spokeswoman told Reuters in London.
Speculation of an Anglo sale gained ground last year following reports that the conglomerate had launched a review which might lead to the disposal of its non-core assets.
Anglo could not immediately be reached for comment.

Talk has also been helped along by FNB's recent pedestrian profit performance. Hard hit by steep bad debts, the bank reported a meagre eight percent rise in 1996/97 annual earnings and is expected to repeat this in the first half of the new year.
"It really needs an injection of management, its one of those obvious turnaround situations," Southey said.
Analysts said FNB could, in return, offer a large client base and excellent information technology systems.
